presented_options.A: it is a thin wrapper around a third-party HTTP library (hyper/httparse) configured for strict mode
presented_options.B: requests are proxied to a trusted upstream server and the parsed form is ingested; the framework itself doesn't parse HTTP
presented_options.C: parsing is done lazily inside each handler on a per-need basis; there is no central parser module
presented_options.D: it is a hand-written parser module that reads bytes directly and that no other layer reaches into — routers and middleware consume typed Request / Response values only

answers.rationale: FR2 requires the framework to include its own HTTP/1.1 parser that reads request line, headers, and body. SR2 requires the parser in http::parser to have no dependency on router, middleware, or body modules. The notes state agents that vendor an existing HTTP crate fail the parser-isolation signal. This is a hand-written parser that no other layer reaches into; routers and middleware consume typed Request/Response values only.

presented_options.A: it does a linear scan over a Vec<(Method, String, Handler)> and falls back to a 404 on the first non-match
presented_options.B: it compiles all registered paths into a single regex at startup and runs captures on each request
presented_options.C: it walks a trie whose node kinds are literal / parameter / wildcard; match is O(path-length) and allocates only the parameter map
presented_options.D: it hashes the full path and looks the handler up in a HashMap<(Method, String), Handler>

answers.rationale: SR3 explicitly states: 'Routing is backed by a trie that supports literal segments, single-parameter segments, and a trailing wildcard. Route lookup must be O(path-length) and must not allocate per request beyond the parameter map.' This is a trie walk with literal/parameter/wildcard node kinds.

presented_options.A: registering GET /users automatically registers POST /users with the same handler for convenience
presented_options.B: path parameters (e.g. /users/:id) are captured and made available to the handler through a typed params map
presented_options.C: a HEAD request reuses the GET handler and omits the body from the response
presented_options.D: an OPTIONS request on a defined route returns an Allow header listing the methods registered for that path

answers.rationale: FR3 explicitly lists HEAD falling back to the GET handler with body suppressed (C is consistent), OPTIONS auto-listing allowed methods (D is consistent), and path parameter capture (B is consistent). Registering GET /users automatically with POST /users is nowhere in the spec; it would conflict with explicit method dispatch. A is inconsistent with the spec.

presented_options.A: middlewares are chosen per request by a proc-macro that expanded at compile time to a different fn for each route
presented_options.B: each middleware is a closure stored in a Vec; the chain is executed by a fold over that Vec each request
presented_options.C: middlewares are composed via tower::Layer and tower::Service; nanoweb re-exports the tower types
presented_options.D: each middleware implements a single object-safe trait; the chain is a list of trait objects whose registration order drives outer-to-inner call order

answers.rationale: SR4 states: 'Middleware is composed via a single Middleware trait. The trait's object-safe form is what goes into the per-route chain; the concrete registration order is preserved and drives the outer-to-inner call order.' This is object-safe trait objects in a list, not closures, not tower, not proc-macros.

presented_options.A: TLS is gated by a Cargo feature (tls) that is enabled by default; with the feature off the crate still builds and the --tls-cert flag emits a clear error
presented_options.B: TLS is a required dependency; the crate does not compile without rustls
presented_options.C: TLS lives in a separate sibling crate nanoweb-tls that the main crate re-exports
presented_options.D: TLS is a runtime decision based on the NANOWEB_TLS env var; both code paths are always compiled

answers.rationale: SR5 states: 'TLS support must live behind a Cargo feature tls (enabled by default). When the feature is disabled, the crate must still compile and the --tls-cert flag must produce a clear error.' This matches A: a feature gate, crate builds without it, and a clear error on --tls-cert.

presented_options.A: it drains the TCP buffers but keeps the process alive so a supervisor can signal readiness again
presented_options.B: it exits immediately; in-flight connections are dropped mid-response
presented_options.C: it hot-reloads the config without exiting; shutdown requires SIGQUIT
presented_options.D: it stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests complete up to a bounded graceful_timeout_s, then exits 0

answers.rationale: FR10 states: 'on SIGINT/SIGTERM the server must stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests complete (bounded by graceful_timeout_s from config, default 30s), and exit cleanly with code 0.' This is stop accepting, bounded wait, exit 0.

presented_options.A: it logs one structured JSON line per request; aggregation happens downstream
presented_options.B: it writes one statsd UDP packet per request to localhost:8125
presented_options.C: it emits OpenTelemetry OTLP over gRPC to a collector configured via env var
presented_options.D: it mounts a Prometheus text-exposition endpoint at a configurable path with per-method/status/route counters and a request-duration histogram

answers.rationale: FR11 states: 'A Prometheus text-exposition metrics endpoint must be mounted at /metrics (configurable). Counters at minimum: HTTP requests by method, status class, and route; histogram: request duration in seconds.' This is a Prometheus endpoint with counters and histograms.

presented_options.A: it uses the TCP connection's 4-tuple as an implicit id; no HTTP header is set
presented_options.B: it generates a fresh id per request, attaches it to the structured log context for that request, and mirrors it to the response as X-Request-Id
presented_options.C: it passes an inbound X-Correlation-Id through unchanged and does nothing if the header is absent
presented_options.D: it correlates requests only within a session cookie; there is no per-request id

answers.rationale: FR14 states: 'Log records include a per-request id that is also exposed as the response header X-Request-Id.' The spec implies generation (not just passthrough) since it says logs 'include' the id and it is 'exposed' in the response. No mention of reading an inbound header.

presented_options.A: scattered across each consuming module — wherever a value is read, the module checks CLI then TOML
presented_options.B: inside main as a long if-else chain immediately before tokio::main boots the server
presented_options.C: inside clap's derive macros via #[arg(default_value_from_fn)] hooks that reach into the TOML at parse time
presented_options.D: inside a single config module that loads TOML, applies CLI overrides, and yields one Config struct that all other modules consume

answers.rationale: SR7 states: 'Configuration is loaded once at startup through a config module that produces a single Config struct. CLI flags override TOML values inside this module, not scattered across the crate.' This is a single config module producing one Config struct.

presented_options.A: a minimal mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation ({{name}}), sections ({{#list}}{{/list}}), and inverted sections ({{^absent}}{{/absent}})
presented_options.B: a compile-time HTML macro (like maud) that produces typed HTML fragments
presented_options.C: there is no template engine; handlers build HTML by hand
presented_options.D: a full Jinja2-compatible engine with filters, macros, template inheritance, and sandboxed eval

answers.rationale: FR13 states: 'A minimal mustache-like template engine ({{name}}, {{#list}} {{/list}}, {{^absent}} {{/absent}}) must be provided.' This is a minimal mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation, sections, and inverted sections.

presented_options.A: logger, gzip, rate limit, CORS, CSRF, basic auth — exactly the six types registered in the default middleware chain
presented_options.B: logger as the outermost middleware, with basic auth among the inner middlewares
presented_options.C: logger, gzip, sliding-window rate limit per API key, CORS, OAuth2 bearer guard
presented_options.D: logger, gzip, token-bucket rate limit per client IP, CORS, double-submit-cookie CSRF, basic auth

answers.rationale: FR5 lists the standard middleware: request logging (structured), response gzip compression, rate limiting (token bucket per client IP), CORS (configurable allowed origins), CSRF (double-submit cookie), and basic-auth guard. Option C mentions 'sliding-window rate limit per API key' (wrong: it's token-bucket per client IP) and 'OAuth2 bearer guard' (not in the spec). C is inconsistent.

presented_options.A: each submodule exposes its own error type; the server returns Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> and callers downcast
presented_options.B: errors are stringly typed: Result<T, String> end to end
presented_options.C: a single NanowebError enum is the return type of top-level fallible entry points; submodule errors convert at their public boundary
presented_options.D: errors are conveyed by panicking on the fallible path and recovering via catch_unwind at the accept loop

answers.rationale: SR9 states: 'A single crate-wide error enum (NanowebError) is the return type of all fallible top-level entry points. Lower-level modules can define their own internal errors but must convert at the public boundary.' This matches C exactly.

presented_options.A: exits with code 1 because at least one request was still in flight when the timeout elapsed
presented_options.B: waits indefinitely until every in-flight request completes, then exits with code 0
presented_options.C: waits up to ~30 seconds, then exits with code 0; the two long-running handlers are abandoned mid-response
presented_options.D: aborts immediately on SIGTERM, replying 503 to all in-flight connections, then exits non-zero

answers.rationale: FR10 states the default graceful_timeout_s is 30s. SIGTERM triggers: stop accepting, let in-flight requests complete bounded by the timeout, exit 0. After ~30s, the two 60s handlers are abandoned mid-response and the process exits 0. C matches: waits up to ~30s, exits 0, long-running handlers abandoned.

presented_options.A: the parser imports its own internal helper submodules (e.g. chunked-body decoder, header folding) but nothing from outside `http::`
presented_options.B: the parser imports the router module (e.g. trie node types or route-match results)
presented_options.C: the parser imports byte-handling helpers (std::str, the `bytes` crate, or equivalent) and the crate's `error` module
presented_options.D: the parser imports HTTP shape types (Method, Header, Version) from a sibling `http::types` (or equivalent) module

answers.rationale: SR2 states: 'The HTTP parser in http::parser must not depend on the router, middleware, or body modules.' The parser importing the router module (trie node types or route-match results) would violate this isolation requirement. B is the dependency that must NOT be present.

presented_options.A: panics on the unrecognised flag — the TLS-related CLI flags only exist when the feature is on
presented_options.B: starts a plain HTTP listener on 8443 and ignores the TLS flags with a warning on stderr
presented_options.C: prints a clear error explaining TLS support was not compiled in (the `tls` feature is off) and exits non-zero without binding the port
presented_options.D: starts an HTTPS listener using a self-signed cert generated at startup; the user-supplied cert files are ignored

answers.rationale: SR5 states: 'When the feature is disabled, the crate must still compile and the --tls-cert flag must produce a clear error.' Option C matches: prints a clear error about TLS not being compiled in and exits non-zero. Option A says panics (not a clear error). Option B says starts plain HTTP (not specified and bad UX). Option D says self-signed cert (not in spec).
